legacy_report:
SOURCE: "Code as Agent Harness: Toward Executable, Verifiable, and Stateful Agent Systems", Xuying Ning, Katherine Tieu, Dongqi Fu, Tianxin Wei, Zihao Li, Yuanchen Bei (core contributors) and ~50 others (UIUC, Meta, Stanford; senior authors Hanghang Tong, Jingrui He); arXiv:2605.18747v1 [cs.CL], 18 May 2026. Preprint. A literature survey, not an experimental paper.

COVERAGE: 102 PDF pages, 358,256 chars extracted. Read pages 1-66 in full (the whole body: intro, sections 2-5, conclusion), about 300k chars. Pages 67-102 are the reference list, which I only grepped for the origins of the harness works below. Nothing was garbled. I stripped short figure-label lines in some chunks, so a few table rows and figure fragments were not read. The survey runs no experiments of its own, so no result table is original to it.

CLAIMS (ranked)
- Definition: a harness is the software layer around the LLM that turns a stateless model into an agent.
  number: none
  setup: framing sentence in the intro, citing [17-23]
  quote: "An agent harness refers to the software layer that surrounds an LLM with tools, APIs, sandboxes, memory, validators, permission boundaries, execution loops, and feedback channels, thereby turning a stateless model into a functional agent capable of long-running task execution"
  where: p.2
- Bottleneck claim: autonomy is limited by the harness as well as by the model.
  number: none
  setup: stated, not measured
  quote: "the bottleneck of autonomy is not only the reasoning ability of the base model, but also the reliability of the system that connects model outputs to long-horizon actions and persistent states."
  where: p.2
- Three coupled elements: model-internal capabilities, system-provided harness infrastructure (the focus of harness engineering [24,25]), and agent-initiated code artifacts (tests, temporary tools, DSL programs, skills). The survey says the third is underexplored.
  number: none
  quote: "System-provided harness infrastructurerefers to the predefined tools, APIs, sandboxes, memory systems, validators, permission boundaries, telemetry, and workflows"
  where: p.2-3
- Code is the harness medium because it is executable, inspectable and stateful.
  number: none
  quote: "Executability means the harness can verify what the model intended. Inspectability means failures can be diagnosed and fed back. Statefulness means the agent's interaction history is not lost between steps."
  where: p.7
- Plan-Execute-Verify (PEV) control loop. The harness acts as a "cybernetic governor". Plans are contracts (files, invariants, validation commands, rollback points). Execution runs in a sandbox with permission tiers. Verification uses deterministic sensors (linters, type checkers, tests, fuzzers, CI).
  number: 3 permission tiers
  quote: "a read-only tier supports repository browsing, retrieval, static inspection, and log analysis; a sandbox-edit tier supports local patching, test execution, and temporary dependency installation inside an isolated workspace; and a full-access tier covers network access, credentials, deployment commands"
  where: p.31 (PEV intro p.28-29)
  Related quotes: "Actions in the final tier should be guarded by mandatory human-in-the-loop (HITL) gates"; "Termination should likewise be governed by verification rather than by model confidence"; "reliability comes from governed state transitions, not simply from better repair prompts."
- Critique should interpret sensors, not replace them: "Compared with natural-language critique, these sensors are deterministic or at least reproducible enough to serve as control signals. Human or agentic critiques remain useful when failure evidence is sparse, but in a governed PEV loop they should interpret sensor outputs rather than replace them" (p.31).
- Tool lifecycle hooks: pre-use hooks validate arguments, enforce permissions and block risky commands. Post-use hooks sanitize output, compact logs, update memory and trigger verification (p.26, p.28).
- Memory is a state-management layer, not a bigger context window or a vector database: "It is a state-management layer that decides which information should remain in the active model context, which information should be compacted into summaries, and which information should be offloaded to durable external storage" (p.22). Compaction example: a failing-test report reduced to test name, key stack frames, suspected files and a link to the full log (p.25).
- Planning artifacts become files: PLAN.md, Implement.md and status logs hold milestones, acceptance criteria, validation commands and recovery rules across context resets, are versioned in Git, and are consumed by subagents (p.19). AGENTS.md-style guidance and MCP registries make actions inspectable before execution (p.30).
- Agentic Harness Engineering (AHE): the harness itself is the optimisation target. Many failures come from the harness, not generation: "many observed failures in code agents arise from missing repository context, brittle tool interfaces, weak validators, excessive token cost, poor retry policies, or mismatched permission boundaries rather than from model generation" (p.32). Deep telemetry feeds an Evolution Agent with a five-stage loop (observe, diagnose, propose, evaluate on held-out or replayed traces, promote only non-regressing changes). Mutations touching permissions, network, credentials or review requirements need HITL approval (p.33).
- Same model, different harness: "even with the same underlying model, repository-level repair performance can vary substantially depending on how interaction state and execution feedback are organized" (SWE-agent, RepairAgent; p.22). Qualitative. No number is given.
- Evaluation conflates model and harness: end-task success "conflate[s] the capabilities of the base model, the quality of the harness, the reliability of tools, the informativeness of feedback, and the difficulty of the environment." It proposes harness-level metrics: trajectory efficiency, verification strength, recovery ability, state consistency, safety compliance, replayability (p.62).
- Green tests can mislead: "a harness can become overconfident precisely because it has executable feedback: the agent sees a green test, but the green test is not the full specification." Every accepted action should carry an evidence bundle (checks run, untested regions, remaining risks) (p.62).
- Failure attribution is weak.
  number: 14-53% best step-level attribution accuracy
  setup: cited studies (Who&When [385], AgenTracer [386], AgentDebug [387])
  quote: "report best step-level attribution accuracies in the 14–53% range, suggesting that production harnesses lack the structured traces needed for principled debugging"
  where: p.52
- Multi-agent: convergence is mostly implicit, which is the field's biggest gap. Examples: ChatDev stops after fixed phases or 10 rounds. AgentCoder is bounded at 5 iterations and Self-Collaboration at 4. Convergence should rest on objective signals (tests, fuzz, performance).
  number: AgentCoder 5 iterations; Self-Collaboration n=4; ChatDev 10 rounds
  quote: "Implicit convergencePipeline termination after a fixed number of stages or iterations with no objective quality criterion is the most prevalent convergence pattern in the literature and represents the most significant gap in the field."
  where: p.46
- AgentCoder's test executor is a deterministic script, not an LLM, and its test designer is independent of the coder (p.37-38).
- Simulated execution can match real execution on some bugs.
  number: 98%+ precision and recall
  setup: QualityFlow imagined execution on MBPP, as reported by the survey. Self-Collaboration's simulated tester is near-identical to its real-compiler ablation.
  quote: "QualityFlow [253] introduces a notable variant: Imagined Execution, in which an LLM simulates the Python interpreter step-by-step and predicts test outcomes without actually running the code, achieving 98%+ precision and recall on MBPP"
  where: p.41, p.47
- Early exit in QualityFlow: "(75–84% of problems converge after the first generator call)" (p.46).
- Production deployment datapoint.
  number: 16.9% fully autonomous, 43.3% with manual intervention
  setup: LingmaAgent at Alibaba Cloud, in-house issues, as reported in cited works [372,373]
  quote: "resolves 16.9% of in-house issues fully autonomously and 43.3% with manual intervention"
  where: p.52
- Other cited numbers, all secondhand and not verified by the survey: MLE-bench bronze on 16.9% of competitions for o1-preview with AIDE, about 3x the next agent (p.59); DiscoveryBench best score about 25% (p.59); El Agente Q above 87% task success on six benchmarks (p.58); A-Lab synthesised 41 of 58 target compounds in 17 days (p.59); OSWorld 369 tasks and AndroidWorld 116 tasks (p.55).
- Harness as distillation surface: production harness traces are now training data, for example Cursor Composer online RL, Codex models trained on harness-like loops. "the boundary between 'the agent' and 'the harness around the agent' is becoming a learnable surface in its own right" (p.52).
- Harness-state findings in multi-agent systems: most systems use implicit, file-only shared state. Topology complexity rises as formal state drops. "Context management is the tax of implicit shared state" (p.47-48). The survey's stated position is that systems need a shared code-centric harness substrate and transactional shared state (p.43, p.64).
- Closing four properties: future systems will be "executable", "inspectable", "stateful" and "governed" (p.66).

LIMITS
- It is a survey with a position, and it reports no controlled experiment of its own. No ablation separates the contribution of the harness from the contribution of the model. "Same model, different harness" appears only as a qualitative remark.
- The authors say planning and memory gains depend on execution conditions, feedback quality and benchmark design, and "reported planning gains may not reflect genuine improvements" (p.20). They say memory conclusions depend on evaluation reliability (p.25).
- Concessions: harness self-evolution is shown only in narrow settings (AutoHarness, AHE, Live-SWE-agent) and stability and rollback are open (p.52-53, p.63). Code-mediated channels "do not eliminate coordination bottlenecks" (p.47). Personalization lacks a reliable oracle (p.61). Verification beyond unit tests is unsolved (p.52).
- The scope is code-centric: "code" is defined broadly (programs, specs, tests, configs, traces), and perception, physical state and intent are explicitly not code (p.7).
- Dated: the cutoff is 2026 and the preprint is v1, so it reads as a snapshot. Vendor material (OpenAI, Anthropic, Cursor, LangChain blogs) is cited only for practice, with no measurements.

BUILDS ON (as printed)
- Harness framing: Lopopolo, OpenAI "Harness engineering: Leveraging codex in an agent-first world", Feb 2026 [16,24]. Trivedy, LangChain "The anatomy of an agent harness", 2026 [25]. Young, Anthropic "Effective harnesses for long-running agents", Nov 2025 [15]. Rajasekaran, Anthropic "Harness design for long-running application development", Mar 2026 [171]. Lin, Cursor "Scaling long-running autonomous coding", Jan 2026 [172].
- Harness optimisation: Lee et al., Meta-Harness, arXiv 2603.28052, 2026 [13]. Lou et al., AutoHarness, arXiv 2603.03329, 2026 [14]. Lin et al., Agentic Harness Engineering, arXiv 2604.25850, 2026 [281]. Pan et al., Natural-Language Agent Harnesses, arXiv 2603.25723, 2026 [173]. Zhou et al., Externalization in LLM agents, arXiv 2604.08224, 2026 [178]. Agrawal et al., GEPA, 2025 [18]. Zhang et al., Agentic Context Engineering, 2025 [17].
- Code-as-reasoning and action lineage: PoT, PAL, Chain of Code, Voyager, SayCan, Code-as-Policies.
- Agent and tool lineage: SWE-agent, OpenHands, ReAct, Reflexion, AgentCoder, MetaGPT, ChatDev, L2MAC, SWE-bench.

CODE: none in the paper beyond one formula. MAGE's score is s(r) = 1 − m(r)/tc(r), where m is mismatches and tc the test cases, iterated until the maximum is 1.0 (p.46). The tool-name list is the HyperAgent navigation tools: "get_tree_structure, go_to_definition, code_search, get_all_references" (p.44).

FIGURES (not rendered; I did not run the figures script, so only caption text was read)
- Fig 1, p.2: taxonomy of code as agent harness (interface, mechanisms, scaling). Fastest map of the survey.
- Fig 8, p.29: PEV loop (Plan: repo maps, specs, invariants, commands. Execute: isolated filesystem, shell, runtime, IDE, permission tiers read-only, sandbox-edit and full-access. Verify: linters, tests, static analysis, stack traces). The most useful figure for the note's constrain/inform/verify/correct framing.
- Fig 9, p.32: AHE loop (replay traces, test held-out tasks, promote verified improvements).
- Fig 4, p.17: roadmap of harness mechanisms, 2023-2026.
- Tables 5-8, pp.23, 27, 30, 34: memory, tool-use, PEV and AHE system lists.

PROBLEMS
- No embedded instructions in the PDF text.
- Text extraction merges words in places (for example "ofagent"). Quotes above were copied as extracted, with spacing artefacts in a few.
- I filtered out short figure and table lines in later chunks, so some table rows were skipped. References (pp.67-102) were only grepped.
- Relation to the target note, which I read only through its front matter and first paragraphs: the note's "Agent = Model + Harness" and four-verb definition (constrain, inform, verify, correct) are not stated in this paper. This paper's definition is the tools/sandboxes/memory/validators/permissions/loops list quoted above, so it sharpens rather than duplicates the note. It cites OpenAI and LangChain as the origin of the harness term. I did not check whether the note's "90% per step, five steps gives about 60%" arithmetic or its Agashe et al. citation appear here; neither does.
